Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB)

Proxy Confidence: Auditing Black-Box LLM Agents with a Surrogate’s Log-Probabilities

Yikai Zhao Affiliation: Amazon Email: yikai@amazon.com    Saurabh Pandey Affiliation: Amazon Email: saurabpd@amazon.com    Pradeep Kumar Misra Affiliation: Amazon Email: pkmisra@amazon.com
Abstract

A deployed LLM agent emits tool calls, queries, and code that can be silently wrong—and by the time the error surfaces, the action has already run. The frontier chat APIs these agents run on offer no reliable way to tell which calls to trust. They hide the model’s own token probabilities. The agent’s stated confidence barely beats chance on the mistakes that matter. And resampling does not help either, since frontier models are now known to be highly repetitive, reproducing the same call across samples.

We recover the missing signal from a low-cost open-weight surrogate run in parallel. It reads the same context, schema, and proposed action as the agent, then scores the call from its own log-probabilities through a family of complementary readouts. Teacher forcing and request-PMI (pointwise mutual information) weigh the likelihood of each argument value; a discriminative verdict judges the call as a whole; tool-choice competition tests the function against its siblings. One principle tells an operator which to trust: a generative likelihood localizes wrong argument values, while the verdict catches holistically wrong calls. When the error type is unknown, an ensemble over the family is the low-regret default—a light logistic combiner, matched by a simple orientation-corrected average. The whole readout is training-free, needs no access to the agent’s internals, and costs one prefill pass in parallel with the tool call.

This proxy ranks correct calls above wrong ones more reliably than either signal a black-box operator has today. Its edge over an agent’s stated confidence is largest exactly where it matters most: on confident mistakes. On difficult coding tasks it reaches AUROC 0.8250.825 where the actor’s own stated confidence is near chance (0.5980.598), and the generative readouts improve on stated confidence by +0.07+0.07 to +0.28+0.28 across the three additional actors we audit. Against self-consistency it gains +0.14+0.14 to +0.19+0.19 on near-deterministic actors, at 1/K1/K the cost of resampling. The signal then drives two deployment modes. A real-time gate escalates an agent’s least-trustworthy calls for human review (+0.05+0.05 to +0.30+0.30 accepted-action accuracy at 50%50\% coverage). And confidence feedback returns the tool result together with the score, so the agent adjusts its own next step; this lifts end-to-end task success on live-execution benchmarks (+0.119+0.119 and +0.137+0.137, both p≤10−4p{\leq}10^{-4}) and beats a random-value control where step errors are silent (+0.078+0.078, p=0.003p{=}0.003).

1 Introduction

Consider a customer-service or data agent running on a frontier chat API. It issues a refund tool call, a database query, or a block of Python. If that action is silently wrong, the cost lands downstream, after execution. The operator would like a confidence signal to gate the action—but in this, the common deployment setting, the two signals a deployer would reach for are both unavailable. (i) The most direct signal, the actor’s own token log-probabilities, is hidden by the frontier chat APIs agents run on. (ii) The standard black-box substitute is self-consistency: resample the actor KK times and measure agreement. It collapses here, because frontier agents are near-deterministic. The actor re-emits the identical call on the overwhelming majority of inputs, leaving almost no sample variance to read—and it costs KK frontier generations to find that out (§4). The actor’s own verbalized self-assessment, meanwhile, is least reliable exactly on its confident mistakes. If we cannot read the actor’s probabilities and it cannot detect its own errors, where should a confidence signal come from?

Our answer is a proxy log-probability. A small, open-weight, log-probability-capable model runs as a training-free sidecar (Figure 1): it reads the same (context,schema,proposed action)(\text{context},\text{schema},\text{proposed action}) the actor conditioned on—no gradient access, no fine-tuning, no actor internals, no shared weights—and emits a scalar confidence. That confidence ranks action correctness better than either black-box baseline (§4). Its edge over the actor’s self-assessment is largest exactly on the actor’s confident mistakes, such as hard code it cannot self-verify. And it significantly beats self-consistency in the near-deterministic regime deployed agents occupy, at 1/K1/K the cost of resampling a frontier model. Because the auditor is a smaller open model its work is a prefill—one forward pass over the already-known action, no autoregressive decode—making it a lightweight, actor-agnostic plug-in for any framework. Cost, latency, and the fail-open guarantee are in §8.

The signal is not monolithic. Which readout to trust has predictable structure, and that structure is what makes the sidecar both cheap and targetable. Every proxy readout is one of two types: a generative likelihood (teacher forcing, or request-PMI, which discounts values the scorer finds likely regardless of the request) or a discriminative decision (a YES/NO verdict, tool-choice competition). This one distinction predicts two things. (a) Which failure mode a readout catches: a generative likelihood reads wrong argument values, tracking judge-free per-parameter accuracy where the verdict is blind to it, while the verdict reads holistic wrongness (§5). (b) Whether a small scorer suffices: teacher forcing is access-bound, equivalence-tested against a scorer twice its size, whereas the verdict is capability-bound and improves with scale (§6). Because the readout type localizes the error, inspecting which readout fires does more than rank reliability—it tells an operator what to look at, turning a scalar into a first diagnosis of the likely failure mode. Even the safe-default fusion can be decomposed into its per-type readouts for that diagnosis. We study function-calling and code agents: their actions are the consequential, error-prone decisions in deployed systems, and their correctness is checkable from the call, context, and schema.

We show that such a sidecar beats the two baselines a black-box deployer would otherwise reach for (§4). Read as a reliability ranking, a small open-weight auditor’s log-probability out-predicts both the actor’s verbalized self-assessment and its self-consistency, and it does so across three actor families. The beats-self margin is regime-graded: the verdict wins in the holistic regime, the generative TF/PMI in argument-value regimes. We then put the readout-type framework to work (§5,6). Because which single readout wins depends on the call’s error locus, an orientation-corrected fusion of the family is the lowest-regret default when that locus is unknown—as it is in deployment. A learned combiner does no better than a simple oriented average.

Finally, we evidence two deployment modes end-to-end (§7). The ranking drives selective prediction on every dataset, needing only an escalation channel. And returning the score to the agent alongside the tool result lifts end-to-end task success on two live-execution benchmarks, beating a random-value control where step errors are silent—a distinction an unannotated control alone would have missed. Throughout, claims are regime-graded and scoped to that class of actions.

2 Background and related work

Confidence estimation for LLMs differs mainly in the source of the signal. Every existing source is unavailable or unreliable once the actor is a deployed, black-box, near-deterministic agent. Actor-internal probabilities. P(True)/self-evaluation reads the model’s probability on its own answer (Kadavath et al., 2022)—intra-model, and inaccessible behind a frontier chat API. Actor verbalized confidence asks the model to state a number (Lin et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024); it is reliable only where the model is well-calibrated, and least reliable exactly on its confident errors. Actor sampling/agreement—self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023), SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al., 2023), semantic entropy (Kuhn et al., 2023; Farquhar et al., 2024)—needs multiple actor samples and collapses under the near-determinism of deployed frontier agents (§4). All three read the actor; none survives the black-box, near-deterministic regime.

A second model as the signal source. LLM-as-judge (Zheng et al., 2023) and cross-examination (Cohen et al., 2023) bring in another model but read its words—a verbalized verdict; weak-to-strong generalization (Burns et al., 2024) and learned process/outcome verifiers (Lightman et al., 2024) require a training step; guardrail classifiers (Inan et al., 2023) screen content, not action correctness. Cross-model likelihood as a metric. Scoring text by a second model’s token log-probabilities is established in generation metrics: BARTScore casts evaluation as generation and reads a scorer model’s likelihood (Yuan et al., 2021), GPTScore steers the same quantity by a natural-language instruction (Fu et al., 2024), while learned MT metrics instead regress on human judgments (Rei et al., 2020); probability-curvature tests read likelihood geometry to detect machine-generated text (Mitchell et al., 2023; Bao et al., 2024). All of these score prose—its fluency, factuality, or provenance—never whether a tool call will execute correctly. And none is organized by which failure mode the readout catches. Our request-PMI readout follows the domain-conditional-PMI correction introduced against surface-form competition in answer scoring (Holtzman et al., 2021), reweighting a likelihood by its context-free prior. Calibration and oversight. Post-hoc calibration sharpens a classifier’s own probabilities (Guo et al., 2017), presuming the access we lack; monitoring an untrusted model with a weaker trusted one is the control-protocol setting (Greenblatt et al., 2024), to which we contribute a concrete training-free monitor signal. We build on standard deployment machinery rather than claim it: accept-if-passes execution-feedback repair (Chen et al., 2024b; Chen et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2023) (self-correction has known limits without an external check (Huang et al., 2024)), selective prediction / risk–coverage (El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017), and cost-driven cascades (Chen et al., 2024a), which our two deployment modes instantiate. The gap we fill: inference-time, training-free, black-box-compatible action verification from a second model’s log-probabilities—not its words, not the actor’s own—organized by a failure-mode map over generative/discriminative readout types.

3 The proxy-confidence sidecar

A black-box actor 𝒜\mathcal{A} emits an action oo and exposes no log-probabilities. A log-probability-capable auditor 𝒮\mathcal{S} (equivalently, the scorer) reads only (context,tool schema,o)(\text{context},\text{tool schema},o)—the same information the actor conditioned on—and computes a scalar confidence (Table 1) at temperature 00. Our primary auditor is a small, open-weight model (Qwen3-32B or 14B, or Gemma-3-27B); this is the cheap-sidecar setting the cost argument (§8) rests on. For the one hard-code case we instead score with a large open-weight model of different lineage than the actor, to rule out same-family self-preference bias; we write 𝒮L\mathcal{S}_{\text{L}} for that scorer and flag it explicitly at that result (§4). Actors are de-identified.11 1 This paper studies a property of the black-box deployment setting—that an actor’s stated confidence is uninformative about its own confident errors—not the standing of any particular vendor’s model. Per-model reliability figures are therefore reported under neutral, de-identified labels, and we make no comparative claim about any provider. All actors are recent instruction-tuned models scored by the same readouts under identical prompts and labels. No claim here needs an actor’s identity to check: each is either within-actor or holds across all actors. We study five actors across three families: A1 and A2, two sizes of a widely deployed closed frontier family; B, a frontier open-weight model; and C-120b/C-20b, two sizes of a second open-weight family. Most analyses use A1 and A2 and add the others to test cross-family generalization (§4); 𝒮L\mathcal{S}_{\text{L}} is of the same lineage as actor B, so for that one result the scorer and an actor share a family, which is why it is never used to score B. The baseline a black-box deployer would otherwise use is 𝒜\mathcal{A}’s own verbalized self-assessment (and, in §4, its self-consistency). Dataset selection. We fix a single a-priori inclusion rule: a benchmark qualifies iff action correctness is checkable by execution/AST/gold-match without an LLM judge. We then take the most widely-used qualifying benchmark in each action category, spanning three model families: function-calling (BFCL (Patil et al., 2025; Patil et al., 2024), xLAM/APIGen (Liu et al., 2024), NESTFUL (Basu et al., 2025)), interactive coding (AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), InterCode nl2bash (Yang et al., 2023)), code generation (LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025), APPS (Hendrycks et al., 2021), CodeContests (Li et al., 2022)), and text-to-SQL (BIRD (Li et al., 2023)). We report on every qualifying benchmark we ran rather than omitting any, including the one regime where the method fails—tau2-bench (Yao et al., 2025), which is omission-dominated and retained as a scope note (§9). Labels are execution/AST/gold-match based per dataset (AppWorld unit tests; BFCL state/response checkers and AST-match; NESTFUL/xLAM gold-call matching; public tests for code; shell-state and file-match for InterCode)—never LLM-judged.

Two primitives.

Every readout is one of two types, and this distinction organizes the paper. A generative readout scores the likelihood the auditor assigns to the action, either raw (teacher forcing, TF) or request-contrasted (request pointwise mutual information, request-PMI). The contrast matters because raw likelihood rewards generic argument values: PMI subtracts the same value’s log-probability with the request withheld, keeping only the evidence the request supplies. A discriminative readout is instead the auditor’s posterior over a discrete label set—over correctness (the verdict) or over function identity (tool-choice competition). The type predicts both the failure mode a signal catches (§5) and whether a small scorer suffices (§6); Table 1 lists the four instances. The verdict needs only generated-token log-probabilities (any chat API that exposes them), whereas TF/PMI require prefill/echo access. We elicit the verdict two ways and report which throughout. Generated-token elicitation reads the log-probability of the scorer’s own next token after the “is this correct?” prompt. Matched elicitation instead forces YES and NO and renormalizes over the pair; because that is the same mechanism as teacher forcing, it is confound-free when we compare the verdict against the generative signals. The two mostly agree, diverging where free-form generation carries formatting cues the forced pair strips out. The divergence is sharpest on xLAM: there the generated-token verdict ties the actor while the matched verdict is near-chance, so the xLAM claim rests on TF/PMI rather than the verdict.

Metric and reporting.

The metric is AUROC for predicting action correctness; significance statements use paired bootstrap over items. We report two quantities and mark them by case: uppercase “PP” is a paired-bootstrap exceedance probability (the fraction of bootstrap resamples in which the proxy signal out-predicts the baseline), and lowercase “pp” is a frequentist test pp-value.22 2 The frequentist test is matched to the contrast: paired-McNemar for a change in end-to-end accuracy over the same items (Mode B, Table 10); Holm-corrected across arms for the multi-arm self-review family (Table 11); and a paired-bootstrap TOST for equivalence claims (§6). Signals are definable on different action types: value-token TF/PMI need a single forced call with JSON arguments, while the verdict applies to any action. Each table therefore reports the datasets/actors/scorers for which its signal is defined and relevant (full coverage matrix, App. G, Table 7). Cross-dataset heterogeneity is high (I2=90%I^{2}{=}90\%), so we report per-dataset AUROC and never pool absolute AUROC. The only pooled numbers are paired contrasts—a within-item sign test of whether the proxy signal out-predicts the same-item baseline—for which level differences cancel. tau2-bench is used only as a scope note, not a per-call benchmark (§9).

4 The sidecar beats the deployer’s two baselines

The deployer’s two black-box options both fail in the deployment regime, and the proxy signal beats each. (1) vs. the actor’s self-assessment. Every proxy readout (§3) reads the scorer’s log-probabilities rather than its words. A within-model mechanism ladder (Figure 2) confirms this is where the signal comes from, and quantifies the payoff. On the same Qwen3-32B we change only the readout—from a verbalized 00–100100 confidence to the verdict token’s log-probability, identical model and prompt content—and AUROC rises +0.09+0.09 to +0.18+0.18 on 5/65/6 datasets (exceedance >0.99>0.99; miss_param, verdict-blind by construction, is the exception at +0.02+0.02). Capability is held exactly constant, so the gain is attributable to access, not scale. The intuition is that a verbalized number is a lossy projection of a model’s internal uncertainty onto a few output tokens, and it is lossy at any scale. Direct log-probability access therefore recovers signal that added capability in the actor cannot—which is why an auditor smaller than the actor can still out-predict its self-report. The payoff follows. Pooled over the five clean datasets where actor self-assessment was logged (AppWorld, BFCL base/long, miss_func, xLAM; n=2439n{=}2439; the verdict-blind miss_param is excluded), the smaller instrumented scorer’s verdict out-predicts the frontier actor’s own self-assessment (pooled paired contrast +0.022+0.022 AUROC, CI95 [+0.002,+0.043][{+}0.002,{+}0.043], P=0.98P{=}0.98—a within-item sign test of direction, not a pooled absolute AUROC). That edge is small but significant overall, and much larger on the individual regimes where the actor is most overconfident. The starkest such regime is hard code, which we show as a separate cross-model judge-solve asymmetry (here the domain-agnostic neutral-verdict scorer 𝒮L\mathcal{S}_{\text{L}}, not the sub-frontier Qwen, scoring actor A1’s LiveCodeBench solutions, n=139n{=}139): the proxy verdict reaches 0.825\mathbf{0.825} while the actor’s own stated confidence is near chance at 0.5980.598 (paired Δ+0.213\Delta{+}0.213, CI95 [+0.13,+0.33][{+}0.13,{+}0.33], P=1.0P{=}1.0). Judging code is easier than writing it and a stated number does not recover that asymmetry: a competent actor can still be an uninformative reporter on its own hardest outputs—the silent-failure regime a guardrail is for, and a property of self-report as a signal source rather than of any one model. That ranking transfers: a calibrator fit on other datasets and evaluated leave-one-dataset-out on held-out LiveCodeBench still scores 0.8360.836 and beats the actor by +0.222+0.222, so the gap is not an overfit artifact (App. E reconciles the three LiveCodeBench verdict figures).

(2) vs. self-consistency—and why the deployment regime is where proxy scoring wins. The other black-box baseline is actor self-consistency (SC): sample the actor K=5K{=}5 times and use output agreement, at K×K{\times} the actor’s cost. SC’s AUROC is governed by the actor’s own sample entropy, so proxy-vs-SC is partly a comparison of actors—which is precisely why proxy scoring wins where agents are deployed. On the near-deterministic actors that dominate deployment (family A, 9494–96%96\% of resampled calls identical) SC has almost no variance to read and falls to 0.570.57–0.620.62, while the proxy generative signal holds 0.720.72–0.770.77 (paired PMI−-SC =+0.19=+0.19 A1, +0.14+0.14 A2, both CI95 excluding 00; SC’s AUROC decays with sample unanimity at r=−0.96r{=}{-}0.96 across five actors, App. E). Near-determinism is a precondition SC needs absent, not an actor defect. We do not claim a blanket win. On higher-entropy actors (family C) SC is competitive (0.760.76–0.810.81), and there neither the best single readout nor a fusion of the applicable readouts (oriented fusion, §5) cleanly beats it. What is unconfounded and universal is the cost asymmetry—one auditor pass vs. KK frontier generations—plus the significant AUROC win in that regime. (On code, cluster-agreement of the samples on the public tests scores 0.720.72–0.840.84, but that runs the test oracle the auditor never sees. Made execution-free to match the auditor’s no-test access it drops to 0.520.52–0.640.64, and the proxy verdict beats it—LiveCodeBench 0.8510.851 vs. 0.6230.623; App. E.)

Auditing generalizes across families; the beats-self margin is regime-graded. We add the three actors outside family A on BFCL (B; C-120b/C-20b), scored by the same Qwen/Gemma auditors—a fully cross-family pairing with no shared weights. The proxy verdict predicts every actor’s turn correctness at AUROC 0.640.64–0.770.77, and is cross-scorer-stable (Qwen≈{\approx}Gemma within ≈0.02{\approx}0.02; Table 6). So auditing generalizes. The beats-self edge is regime-graded, and the two readout types split it cleanly along the failure-mode map we develop next (§5). The discriminative verdict beats self on family A’s holistic BFCL regime, but only ties on B and C, which self-assess well there (0.660.66–0.770.77). The generative TF/PMI beats self on the argument-value regime for all three of the remaining actors: teacher-forcing each of their xLAM calls through the proxy Qwen3-32B, request-PMI predicts correctness at 0.720.72–0.790.79 and improves on the actor’s own stated confidence by +0.07+0.07 to +0.28+0.28, all significant (Table 2). The margin is large where the actor states confidence near chance (0.510.51–0.530.53), and smaller but still significant where the actor self-assesses well at 0.650.65 yet still loses to PMI. Whether the proxy signal beats an actor’s verbalized self-assessment thus depends on the actor’s self-calibration and on the regime. We report that as a family/regime-graded effect rather than universal dominance. Because the auditor is open, it also admits an epistemic readout a black-box pipeline cannot: ensemble disagreement between two different-lineage scorers (0.700.70–0.800.80, near-free; App. K).

Taken together: auditing generalizes. A proxy log-probability ranks correctness across three unrelated actor families with no shared weights, and across action types (tool calls and code; §4, §7). Beating the actor’s own confidence, by contrast, is regime-graded—strongest exactly where the actor is blind to its own errors. The sidecar is not a universal oracle. It is a guardrail whose edge grows with the actor’s error rate, scoped to actions whose correctness is decidable by reading them (§9)—precisely the regime a deployer cares about.

5 The signal family and its failure-mode map

Log-probability access buys more than one signal. We state a failure-mode map a priori—which readout should win on which action type—and then test it (Table 3; the same matrix as a heatmap is in App. K, Fig. 5). The champion signal marches predictably from the verdict on coarse holistic regimes to teacher forcing on argument-heavy ones to tool-choice competition on wrong-function risk.

Verdict—holistic correctness (the default).

Where correctness is adjudicable on-face, the one-token verdict is cheapest and best (AppWorld 0.8940.894 vs. actor 0.7880.788, P=.996P{=}.996; BFCL base/long), and on AppWorld beats a trajectory-length baseline the actor’s self-report does not—diagnostic, not a length proxy.

Teacher forcing / request-PMI—when argument values carry the risk.

Here the holistic verdict is too coarse. On NESTFUL, TF (0.6430.643) beats the verdict (0.5940.594, P=.98P{=}.98). On miss_param (a required argument withheld) the verdict is at chance (0.5170.517) while TF recovers 0.5730.573 and beats the actor, and the ranking is actor-invariant (A2: TF 0.604>0.604> verdict 0.552>0.552> self 0.5940.594). A judge-free anchor confirms the mechanism: against deterministic per-parameter accuracy, TF’s correlation rises to ρ=0.41\rho{=}0.41 as the target sharpens to argument values, while the verdict collapses to ρ=0.02\rho{=}0.02—for both actors (App. K, Fig. 6). On short structured calls (BFCL v3) request-PMI (0.7140.714) ties the verdict. And for wrong-function risk (miss_func) a counterfactual over k=4k{=}4 sibling tools reaches 0.6810.681 where the verdict is weak (0.5920.592).

Fusion—additive when signals are complementary, and orientation is mandatory.

We write oriented fusion for the orientation-corrected rank-average of whichever readouts are defined on a given call—in practice verdict++TF, plus PMI or tool-choice where they apply. (A larger full-battery fusion of all 16 single-pass readouts is an appendix probe, App. D.) Verdict and TF are nearly orthogonal (ρ≤0.36\rho{\leq}0.36), so rank-averaging helps most where they catch different errors: miss_param (0.517/0.573→0.6970.517/0.573{\to}0.697 learned, ≈0.62{\approx}0.62 plain rank-average, beating either and the actor), parallel (0.6950.695), NESTFUL (0.6550.655). It is not free: where signals share errors it does not exceed the best single readout, and PMI on top of verdict++TF hurts on nested args (0.655→0.6250.655{\to}0.625). Two rules govern it. First, the combiner barely matters—a learned logistic is indistinguishable from an orientation-corrected rank-average, so we claim no trained combiner (App. D). Second, orientation is essential, and free: some TF signals are anti-correlated with correctness in a regime. This happens when the fluent, high-likelihood completion is the wrong one—the scorer finds a generic or default-valued call likelier than a correct call needing an unusual argument, so higher TF flags the easy-but-wrong action. A naïve average that fails to flip such a signal can fall below chance, so we fit each sign on a held-out fold.

Which signal to trust is therefore not a mystery. The failure-mode map makes it predictable from where the error can live—generative for argument values, discriminative for holistic wrongness. Two operational questions follow, and the same generative/discriminative split answers both: does the sidecar need a large scorer, and can it run cheaply?

6 Which readout, how cheap, and when to specialize

The generative/discriminative type answers the first of the two questions §5 closed on, and the answer makes the sidecar cheap.

Teacher forcing == access-bound: a 14B suffices (equivalence-tested). We re-score every dataset with Qwen3-14B (bf16)—half the 32B’s parameters, every signal through the identical prefill on both scorers. The teacher-forcing readout is capability-invariant: on all six matched cells the 14B tracks the 32B within |Δ|≤0.015|\Delta|{\leq}0.015 AUROC (on xLAM the 14B is fractionally ahead), and a paired-bootstrap TOST equivalence test (δ=0.05\delta{=}0.05) passes on all 66 (App. H, Fig. 4). Reading an action’s raw likelihood needs log-probability access, not scale: the quantity is intrinsic to the forward pass over low-entropy value tokens. Request-PMI contrasts two prefills and is more scale-sensitive than raw TF (−0.04-0.04–0.050.05 at 14B on the two cells we test), so we treat the 14B-suffices claim as specific to teacher forcing. Discriminative == capability-sensitive: the verdict falls on the other side. Elicited the same way on both scorers (confound-free), the 32B verdict significantly beats the 14B on 66 of 99 matched dataset×\timesactor cells (90% CI excludes 0; none favor the 14B). The three exceptions are the two NESTFUL cells and AppWorld, where trajectory correctness is legible even to the small scorer; Table 8 shows representative cells. The mechanism is a difference in kind: a generative likelihood is intrinsic to the forward pass, whereas the verdict must instantiate a learned decision boundary over an abstract correctness latent—a meta-competence that scales with capability. With n=2n{=}2 sizes we report this as a capability trend, not an invariance law. Deployment consequence: provision a 1414B scorer for access-bound teacher forcing, and add the 3232B when the verdict, request-PMI, or a fusion including them carries weight.

Robustness: not one pairing. A 2×2×32{\times}2{\times}3 grid (A1/A2 ×\times Qwen3-32B/Gemma-3-27B ×\times AppWorld/BFCL base/long; Table 6) shows the verdict is not a Qwen artifact. The two different-lineage scorers agree within ≈0.02{\approx}0.02 AUROC on BFCL (and ≈0.06{\approx}0.06 on AppWorld), and both beat both actors’ self-assessment (exceedance >0.99>0.99 against the stronger A2). The lone exception is AppWorld×\timesA2, a strong self-assessor on its own long code trajectory. The cross-family evidence for families B and C (Tables 2, 6) was presented in §4.

7 From confidence to action: two deployment modes

The ranking is directly useful in two modes (Figure 1). Mode A—selective prediction—is the uniform, always-available use. Ranking calls by proxy confidence and accepting only the most-confident fraction (abstaining/escalating the rest) improves accepted-action accuracy on every dataset—a direct consequence of AUROC>0.5{>}0.5 (per-dataset numbers in Table 5, App. C). At 50%50\% coverage on natural errors, accepted accuracy rises +0.05+0.05 (BFCL), +0.16+0.16 (xLAM), and +0.095+0.095 on tau2 (scored at the trajectory level against end-to-end task success, not per call). On the injected-error needle construction—which corrupts exactly one call per trajectory and asks the signal to localize it—accuracy rises +0.22+0.22–0.300.30. The risk–coverage area is far below random abstention everywhere. Needing only an abstain/escalate channel and no self-repairing actor, Mode A is the one use that works on any black-box agent. It can also buy efficiency rather than accuracy: at a fixed audit budget of one call per trajectory, ranking by proxy confidence repairs the injected error 0.920.92 of the time on xLAM and 0.650.65 on NESTFUL, versus 0.420.42/0.400.40 for a random-call budget (p<10−4p{<}10^{-4}, p=0.008p{=}0.008), so it decides where to spend review even where blanket review saturates. (Handing the actor its own confidence post hoc to self-correct helps only where it cannot otherwise self-verify the call; App. J. tau2 probes an orthogonal omission-dominated regime and is a scope note, §9.)

Mode B—confidence feedback: return (result,c)(\text{result},c) and let the actor act. The most direct use of the hook is the one Figure 1 draws: append the confidence to the tool result the actor reads next, and let it choose its own next move—no gate, no human. With an A2 actor, oriented fusion raises end-to-end task success on both live-execution benchmarks: nl2bash (Yang et al., 2023) 0.399→0.5180.399{\rightarrow}0.518 (+0.119+0.119; 2929 tasks rescued vs. 66 broken, exact p=10−4p{=}10^{-4}; n=193n{=}193) and AppWorld test_challenge 0.595→0.7310.595{\rightarrow}0.731 (+0.137+0.137; 100/43100/43, p<10−4p{<}10^{-4}; n=417n{=}417).

Two controls then separate the benchmarks, and that split is the point. Announcing an audit while withholding the number does nothing (nl2bash −0.010-0.010, p=0.87p{=}0.87); an independent U⁡(0,1)U(0,1) draw is likewise flat (+0.041+0.041, p=0.28p{=}0.28), and fusion beats that draw by +0.078+0.078 (19/419/4, p=0.003p{=}0.003)—so here the annotation’s content matters, not merely its presence. AppWorld inverts this: the random stream matches fusion (+0.005+0.005, 46/4446/44, p=0.92p{=}0.92) and the displayed signal sits at chance (AUROC 0.390.39–0.470.47 vs. 0.640.64). The reason is diagnostic—AppWorld’s Python failures mostly raise, so the traceback already carries the diagnosis, whereas on nl2bash half of all wrong steps emit no error text at all. Mode B therefore earns its keep only where step errors are silent—and a random-value arm is what tells an operator which of the two regimes they are in (App. J).

8 Deploying the sidecar: cost, latency, and the safe default

Why the sidecar is cheap: the scorer’s work is a prefill.

The confidence readouts are dominated by prefill, not autoregressive decode. Teacher-forcing the actor’s already-known action needs one forward pass over known tokens with zero generation; request-PMI needs two; the verdict needs one prefill plus a single token. The scorer never pays the long decode the actor already paid, so a 1414B pass over the shared context is cheaper than the actor’s own generation—and than the KK frontier generations SC needs. “Lightweight” here means per-call compute; the sidecar is still a second model to host. A generative-only deployment is cheapest, since a 1414B suffices for the access-bound signals, while a verdict/fusion gate provisions the 3232B (§6). Measured on the deployed 1414B fp8 sidecar at realistic full-context length (one L40S GPU, Table 9), a scored call takes 123123–159159 ms at the median (p​99≤179p99{\leq}179 ms). That is a single-digit-percent addition to the 100100s-of-ms a real tool call (DB query, API round-trip) already costs, and it is hidden entirely when the scorer runs concurrently with execution. Scoring is triggered by the framework’s pre-execution tool-call hook, which already holds the (context,schema,action)(\text{context},\text{schema},\text{action}) tuple, so it needs no extra actor calls, adds ≈0{\approx}0 to the Mode A critical path, and fails open on timeout so the guardrail can never stall the agent. Because the hook fires per call, scoring can be restricted to high-stakes calls: as a design policy (not a measured cost-saving) a static allowlist of writes/refunds/deletes plus a free-form-argument heuristic routes argument-bearing calls to TF/PMI. The evidenced selectivity is that the signal tells you where to spend a fixed review budget once calls are scored (§7).

Oriented fusion is the regime-agnostic safe default.

The failure-mode map (§5) says which single signal wins in each regime. But exploiting it requires knowing the error locus a priori, which is exactly the deployment knowledge a black-box operator usually lacks. Worse, every single signal has a catastrophic regime. The verdict is near-blind where a required argument is withheld (miss_param 0.5170.517, at chance), and teacher forcing is weak on the coarse holistic calls the verdict handles best (BFCL v3 0.5490.549 vs. the 0.7140.714 optimum there). Committing to either one blind therefore risks a large loss. We quantify this as worst-case regret: the AUROC gap between a fixed policy and the best-achievable signal in each regime. Reading the oriented fusion caps worst-case regret at 0.019\mathbf{0.019} AUROC (mean 0.0070.007), versus ≈0.17\approx 0.17–0.180.18 for either single-signal policy (breakdown in Table 4, App. B).

Fusion or a single signal? A practitioner’s rule.

The choice is risk management, not performance maximization: default to oriented fusion whenever you cannot predict, per call, where the error will be—the common black-box case. Fusion is not the highest-ceiling readout in any regime but the lowest-floor one, the only choice independent of the call pattern. Drop to a single signal only when you know the error locus a priori: a verdict for holistic correctness, teacher-forcing/request-PMI when argument values carry the risk, tool-choice competition for wrong-function routing. Each is cheaper, and ties or edges fusion where you are right about the locus. The deployable edge tracks the actor’s error rate. It is largest on error-prone tool/code regimes (AppWorld +0.11+0.11, BFCL, NESTFUL, miss_param), and slightly negative only for the verdict on easy xLAM (−0.06-0.06, where TF/PMI still lead)—exactly the calls the actor already gets right, which least need a guardrail.

9 Limitations and scope

Our claims are scoped to actions whose correctness is decidable by reading them—for a tool call, whether it matches the request and schema. Where the deciding evidence is an external fact absent from the context, we claim nothing. One hazard carries into deployment: a readout’s sign is regime-dependent. Teacher forcing anti-correlates with correctness wherever the fluent completion is the wrong one (§5), so orientation must be fit on held-out labels per regime and never ported; an unvalidated sign gives an anti-correlated gate, not merely a weak one. The beats-self edge is regime/family-graded, not universal—on BFCL outside family A the verdict only ties (§4)—and a second strong closed frontier family is untested. The cost claim rests on a 1/K1/K-generations plus smaller-model argument and single-GPU latency (Table 9); multi-tenant serving is unprofiled and scorer size spans only a 2×2\times ratio (≤\leq8B untested). Learned fusion does not beat an orientation-corrected rank-average (App. D), so we claim no trained calibrator. Finally, Mode B is regime-dependent: it beats a random-value control only where step errors are silent (§7), so it warrants a scorer-validity check Mode A does not.

Appendix D Coverage vs. the combiner (battery detail)

Given a battery, the combiner barely matters but orientation is essential (§5). On the one richly-instrumented, validly-labeled dataset we can test it (BFCL v3, proxy 32B scorer, n=216n{=}216), the full 16-readout single-pass battery reaches 0.7640.764 vs. 0.7060.706 for the verdict++TF pair (Δ=+0.059\Delta{=}{+}0.059, one-sided p=0.028p{=}0.028; two-sided CI95 [−0.001,+0.119][{-}0.001,{+}0.119] grazes 00)—suggestive, not confirmed. The combiner choice is not distinguishable: a learned logistic scores 0.7330.733 against 0.7640.764 for the orientation-corrected rank-average, with a CI95 crossing 00. A permutation test (shuffled labels) collapses the learned OOF to 0.500.50, so there is no leakage. The larger tau2 battery result of prior drafts is withdrawn: tau2 lacks a per-call correctness oracle (§9). On the 4-signal xLAM/NESTFUL cells, where few readouts are defined, the full set only ties verdict++TF (Δ≤+0.025\Delta{\leq}{+}0.025). Per-argument-count (xLAM): the learned lift over rank-average is significant on multi-argument calls (CI90 [+0.010,+0.044][{+}0.010,{+}0.044]) but null on single-argument calls ([−0.002,+0.032][{-}0.002,{+}0.032])—one value-token readout already dominates there.

Appendix E Actor self-consistency: detail

Self-consistency (SC) == plurality agreement of K=5K{=}5 temp-0.80.8 samples (name++canonicalized args), execution-free; the label is the gold-match correctness of the deployed temp-00 call (leave-base-out, non-circular). SC’s AUROC as a correctness predictor decays monotonically with how unanimous the actor’s samples are (r=−0.96r{=}{-}0.96 across five actors from three families; Figure 3). Near-deterministic frontier actors therefore drive SC to chance. On the ∼95%\sim\!95\% of xLAM problems where the KK samples are unanimous, SC carries zero signal by construction, yet the proxy TF signal still discriminates at 0.720.72. Code execution artifact. Cluster-agreement of the KK samples on the public tests scores 0.720.72–0.840.84 on code_contests/APPS, but that implicitly runs the public-test oracle the proxy signal never sees. Made execution-free (agreement on normalized code text), it drops to 0.520.52–0.640.64 on all three code datasets, and on A1 the proxy verdict beats it (LiveCodeBench 0.8510.851 vs. 0.6230.623). (The three LiveCodeBench verdict figures measure different comparisons on this same regime: 0.8250.825 vs. actor self-assessment, n=139n{=}139 (§4); 0.8360.836 under leave-one-dataset-out transfer; and 0.8510.851 here on the SC-comparison subset.)

Appendix J Feeding the signal back to the actor (self-review detail)

Beyond selective escalation (Mode A) and confidence feedback (Mode B), we tested handing the actor its own proxy confidence to self-correct. The protocol keeps the actor black-box: it completes its trajectory; the Qwen3-32B auditor scores every call; the actor is then shown its calls annotated with per-call signals and re-emits a corrected sequence. Arms differ only in the annotation: blind (none), verdict/tf/fusion/all, and placebo. The placebo shows the same numbers deranged onto the wrong calls—identical flag budget, wrong positions—which makes it the decisive control: it separates localized information from a mere look-again nudge.

The boundary is whether the actor can self-verify the call at review time (Table 11). Take single-shot xLAM first, where correctness is legible only from the schema. There, showing the signal beats unaided review on the A1 reviewer (Holm p=0.004p{=}0.004 vs. blind), and beats the deranged placebo on both reviewers (A1 p=0.013p{=}0.013, A2 p=0.006p{=}0.006). The gain is therefore localized information rather than a look-again nudge. On A2 the vs-blind margin is directional but not significant after correction. NESTFUL (recompute) and live BFCL-v4 (re-read real tool output) go the other way: unaided review already captures the gain, and no signal arm beats blind or placebo. These negatives share one cause, and it is the boundary itself—when the actor can cheaply self-verify the call from the real result, a proxy number adds little beyond unaided reflection. The same boundary separates our two inline benchmarks below.

Mode B in full: the readouts in a live loop. Detail behind §7’s Mode B—appending each step’s confidence to its real tool result, so the actor sees it in context on every observation and may adjust its next action. We compare the readouts of §5 against three controls: an unannotated run, a vigilance arm that announces the audit but shows no number, and a random arm that shows an independent U⁡(0,1)U(0,1) draw in place of the real confidence (Table 10).

On InterCode nl2bash [Yang et al., 2023] the readouts order as §5 predicts. All arms cover the same 193 usable tasks (200 minus 7 whose gold command fails its own grader) and every contrast is paired. Announcing an audit without showing a number does nothing (0.3890.389, −0.010-0.010, p=0.87p{=}0.87), so any effect requires the number itself. The discriminative verdict alone does not separate (0.4300.430, +0.031+0.031, p=0.36p{=}0.36). The generative likelihoods do: request-PMI reaches 0.4720.472 (+0.073+0.073, 25/11, p=0.029p{=}0.029) and teacher forcing 0.4970.497 (+0.098+0.098, 25/6, p=0.001p{=}0.001). Strongest is the oriented fusion at 0.5180.518 (+0.119+0.119, 29 rescues vs. 6 regressions, exact p=10−4p{=}10^{-4}, bootstrap 95% CI [+0.062,+0.176][{+}0.062,{+}0.176]). The generative-over-discriminative ordering and the fusion’s low-regret behaviour were both established offline as ranking properties (§5, §6); here they reappear in a live loop. Read against the random arm below, only the generative readouts and their fusion clear its 0.4400.440—the verdict arm (0.4300.430) does not reach it. The separation that survives a noise control is therefore specifically the generative one.

On nl2bash the random arm rules out the trivial explanation that any number in the loop makes the actor more careful: an independent U⁡(0,1)U(0,1) draw does not significantly beat the unannotated control (0.4400.440, +0.041+0.041, 25/17, p=0.28p{=}0.28), and fusion beats it by +0.078+0.078 (19/4, p=0.003p{=}0.003, CI [+0.031,+0.124][{+}0.031,{+}0.124]). A meaningless scalar is therefore not sufficient: the annotation’s content matters relative to noise. We state the claim at that level deliberately. The real and random streams differ in more than one respect—in where their low values fall, and in how they are scaled. (Fusion occupies a narrow band, mean 0.6360.636, sd 0.1440.144, while the uniform draw has twice the spread and dips below 0.100.10 on 9%9\% of steps.) The comparison therefore does not by itself identify which property drives the effect, so we report the end-to-end result and leave the causal decomposition to future work.

AppWorld test_challenge (417 tasks, 139 scenarios) shows the opposite pattern, and the contrast is the point. Inline fusion gains +0.137+0.137 over the unannotated control there (100100/4343, p<10−4p{<}10^{-4}). But so does the random arm, by +0.132+0.132 (9595/4040, p<10−4p{<}10^{-4}), and the two are indistinguishable (+0.005+0.005, 4646/4444, p=0.92p{=}0.92; cluster-robust 95% CI [−0.043,+0.053][{-}0.043,{+}0.053], and +0.008+0.008, p=0.81p{=}0.81, on the 390 tasks where our step cap forced neither label). On that benchmark any scalar suffices: we detect no contribution from the readout’s content. Reporting only the vs-control number would have made AppWorld look like a second confirmation; the random arm shows it is not one.

What distinguishes nl2bash is the shape of its failures: its answers are md5 sums, counts and file listings, so a subtly wrong pipeline returns a well-formed, plausible, wrong value. Classifying every executed step of the benchmark’s published reference trajectories (n=1176n{=}1176), 50%50\% of wrong steps are silent—clean, non-empty output with no error text—and 48%48\% of episodes contain at least one such step (a proxy for our actor’s error profile rather than a direct measurement of it). There is no traceback for a reviewer to restate, so an external judge adds information the actor cannot obtain from its own observation. (Our unannotated control scores 0.3990.399, below the 0.4850.485 the benchmark reports for its own published reference actor. Two harness choices account for the gap. The first is an 8-turn cap per task. The second is rewriting leading-cd compound commands as subshells, to work around a path-handling bug in the environment that prevents the working directory from persisting. Both apply identically to every arm, so they depress absolute success uniformly and leave the paired contrasts unaffected.)

The two benchmarks also differ in the signal’s measured validity, in the same direction. On AppWorld the displayed inline confidence has no task-level validity on this split (AUROC 0.3880.388 mean-pooled, 0.4740.474 min-pooled—at or below chance, and below a trajectory-length baseline at 0.6080.608), against 0.640.64 on nl2bash. This is a different quantity from the AppWorld verdict of Table 3 (0.8940.894): that is a per-call verdict AUROC on the standard split, whereas this is the task-level pooled validity of the displayed fusion on test_challenge under the revised scorer prompt. The per-call readout retains its ranking power; what fails is its aggregation to a task-level target on this split. The reason is structural: AppWorld steps execute Python whose failures mostly raise, so the diagnostic information is already in the observation the actor reads. A scorer-prompt revision that removed a measured position artifact there (confidence–step-index correlation +0.60→+0.15+0.60\rightarrow+0.15, reaching parity between mandatory setup steps and substantive actions) succeeded mechanically yet bought zero predictive power. That locates the failure in the target rather than the prompt. The operational reading is this: the readout’s content earns its cost only where the environment does not already surface its own errors. An inline number may still raise accuracy elsewhere, as it does on AppWorld, but then any scalar would do. A random-value arm is what tells an operator which case they are in.

Taken together, Mode B raises end-to-end accuracy on both live-execution benchmarks (+0.119+0.119 and +0.137+0.137, both p≤10−4p{\leq}10^{-4}). But only on nl2bash does that gain depend on what the number says. The dividing line is whether the environment already surfaces its own errors, and it coincides with the signal’s measured validity (0.640.64 vs. chance). One evaluation lesson generalizes: for such loops an unannotated control is not sufficient, and a random-value arm is the minimum. “Beats no annotation” and “beats noise” are different claims, and on one of our two benchmarks they come apart.

Appendix K Signals beyond the single-pass family, and the judge-free anchor

Because the auditor is open it admits four readouts a black-box pipeline cannot compute (Table 12). Ensemble disagreement—−|qQwen−qGemma|-|q_{\text{Qwen}}{-}q_{\text{Gemma}}| between different-lineage scorers—is a strong standalone signal (0.700.70–0.800.80) and near-free. Semantic entropy of regenerations (0.680.68–0.710.71) tracks self-consistency but does not exceed single-pass signals. Schema-satisfaction is null on frontier actors (0.500.50–0.510.51), which emit schema-valid calls ∼\sim100% of the time. Two verdict elaborations mostly do not beat the one-token verdict. A debiased verdict (symmetric double-ask) does not improve on tool calls (BFCL v3 0.6700.670 vs. 0.7110.711). A multi-axis verdict helps only on long code: on LiveCodeBench it gains (0.8180.818 vs. plain 0.7830.783), whereas on BIRD text-to-SQL it trails (0.6480.648 vs. 0.6700.670), both same-file comparisons. So the single-token verdict is a strong, cheap default, and elaborations pay off only when the extra axes carry independent information.
